title: Why Can't I See the Numbers Now?

patient.name: Mr Chua Kok Wai
patient.presenting_complaint: Recently finds it harder to tell some colours apart, mainly in the left eye

history.hpc: Mr Chua reports a recent change: 'Last time I never have problem with colour, why now cannot see some number?' He notices it more with the left eye and says colours look 'washed out' on that side. He is diabetic. No eye pain, but he has had some blurring of the left eye. The recent onset and the difference between the two eyes are notable.
history.pmhx: Type 2 diabetes (sub-optimal control). No previous eye surgery.
history.family_hx: No known colour blindness in the family
history.social_hx: Warehouse supervisor. Non-smoker. Reports irregular diabetic follow-up.

examination_findings.fundus: Diabetic retinopathy changes possible; left eye reduced VA and colour change — for dilated doctor review

investigations.colour_vision_ishihara: Ishihara plates tested for EACH eye separately and documented as plates read correctly per eye. Result: right eye reads most plates; left eye reads noticeably fewer. An asymmetric, recently-acquired colour defect (worse in one eye) differs from congenital red-green deficiency, which is usually symmetrical and lifelong.

diagnosis: An asymmetric, recently-acquired colour vision defect (worse in the left eye) with reduced left VA in a diabetic patient — unlike a congenital colour deficiency, this pattern suggests an acquired ocular cause and needs doctor review. The competency is testing each eye separately, documenting correctly, and recognising acquired versus congenital patterns.

immediate: Test colour vision with the Ishihara chart for EACH eye separately (acquired defects can be asymmetric)
Document the number of plates read correctly for each eye
Note the recent onset and the difference between the eyes as features of an acquired defect
Perform VA for each eye and note the reduced left VA
Flag the asymmetric, acquired colour change and reduced VA to the doctor for review
Ensure good lighting and avoid coaching during the test
follow_up: Doctor to assess for an ocular cause (e.g., diabetic eye disease, optic nerve or macular cause), likely with dilation/imaging
Encourage the patient to resume regular diabetic eye follow-up
Document and hand over the per-eye results
patient_education: Explain that testing each eye separately helps show that the change is mainly in one eye
Explain that a recent, one-sided colour change is different from being colour blind from birth and should be checked
Encourage better diabetic control and regular eye follow-up
Reassure him the doctor will review the eye to find the cause

key_points: Establishes the recent onset of the colour change (not lifelong)
Identifies the asymmetry (worse in the left eye) and associated blurring
Notes the diabetes and irregular follow-up as relevant context
Confirms no family history of colour blindness
Tests the Ishihara chart for each eye separately
Documents plates read correctly per eye
Performs VA for each eye and notes the reduced left VA
Ensures good lighting and avoids coaching
Recognises an asymmetric, recently-acquired colour defect differs from congenital
Links the colour change with reduced VA in the same (left) eye
Considers an acquired ocular cause in a diabetic patient
Knows this warrants doctor review rather than reassurance
Documents per-eye Ishihara and VA results clearly
Flags the acquired, asymmetric pattern to the doctor
Encourages diabetic control and regular eye follow-up
Explains the findings to the patient in simple terms
